headline: Birds Know No Borders: Why Global Protection Matters
meta_description: Alex Ngari explains why protecting migratory birds requires international cooperation across Africa, Europe, and Asia—and how wetland loss threatens millions.
summary_short: Migratory birds traveling between continents need coordinated protection across borders, says BirdLife Africa's Alex Ngari. But wetland loss threatens critical stopover…
body:
Millions of birds belonging to hundreds of species make an extraordinary journey twice yearly, flying between breeding grounds in Europe and Asia and wintering habitats across Africa. Yet scientists possess surprisingly limited knowledge of where exactly these birds travel—or what dangers they face along the way. This gap in understanding has real consequences: without knowing a bird's complete migratory cycle, conservationists cannot effectively protect them. According to Alex Ngari, migratory birds and flyways programme manager for BirdLife Africa, the solution requires a fundamental shift in how we think about conservation. "Migratory birds do not belong to any one country, but are a shared global heritage, and their survival requires a borderless safety net," Ngari explains. "These birds know no borders, which means that every country has a responsibility to protect them."

The immediate threat is clear: since the 1970s, approximately 22 percent of Africa's wetlands have vanished due to human encroachment, climate change, and unsustainable water extraction. Lake Chad stands as a stark example. Birds crossing the vast Sahara Desert depend on this lake to rest, feed, and drink—yet 90 percent of it has already disappeared. Similarly, the Tana River Delta in Kenya faces threats from farming and proposed dam construction, while Rwanda's Nyabarongo Wetlands suffer from agricultural activity and papyrus extraction. The Bijagós Archipelago in Guinea-Bissau, which hosts over one million wintering birds annually, confronts rising sea levels and overfishing that reduces available food.

BirdLife has identified 471 priority conservation sites across the Africa-Eurasian Flyway, but protecting them requires coordination that transcends national boundaries. Without detailed knowledge of migration routes, conservation strategies risk benefiting some species while inadvertently harming others. As electronic tracking technology becomes more accessible, researchers are finally gathering precise data about these journeys—yet the real work lies ahead: ensuring that every nation along these ancient routes recognizes its shared responsibility to these extraordinary travelers.
quick_facts: 22% of Africa's wetlands have disappeared since the 1970s
Lake Chad has lost 90% of its surface area
Bijagós Archipelago hosts over one million wintering birds yearly
471 priority sites identified across the Africa-Eurasian Flyway
Migratory birds travel between Europe, Asia, and Africa twice yearly
